rationale: All three lenses ran with parseable output against a present spec; 17 blocking findings survive triage (4 critical: unsanitized attacker-controlled state reaching two callback log lines (AC7 fail), an unguarded authorize-URL parse that turns a successful initiate into a 500 (AC8 partial), the discovered/recovery paths not emitting the joinable auth_config_id key (AC1 partial), and a waited_ms cross-repo contract mismatch that silently 422s the timeout beacon (AC6 partial)). Confidence is low because one decision_needed item remains: whether the timeout beacon can carry a state prefix depends on whether the UI hook has access to the state, which needs a human call. 2 findings deferred as pre-existing and not emitted - (a) the /callback-diagnostics route is unauthenticated and unthrottled, which this change makes alert-visible but did not introduce, and (b) _sanitize_log_value does not escape quotes/backslashes for JSON-by-interpolation log formats, a pre-existing weakness of the moved helper; 9 findings dismissed, including the pydantic details leak and the doubled /v1 beacon URL, both disproved by orchestrator-verified evidence.

business_review.item: AC1 - every initiate path (static, discovered, recovery, SAML) emits one structured INFO carrying flow kind, mcp_config_id, auth_config_id, discovered_flow_id, user_id, state prefix, client_id, authorize host, redirect_uri, resource, scope
business_review.notes: All four INFO lines exist (_initiate.py:116, 234, 320, 418) and are asserted by tests. But the discovered line names the auth-config id `discovered_auth_id=` (_initiate.py:236) while _discovery.py:215 and _oauth2_callback.py:522 emit the same value as `auth_config_id=` (confirmed: codemie_enterprise/mcp_auth/discovered_flow.py:350 sets resolution.auth_config_id = discovered_auth_id); the recovery line omits auth_config_id entirely (_initiate.py:320-325).

business_review.item: AC2 - discovered flows additionally log issuer, registration_method, registration_reason_code, registration_profile_fingerprint
business_review.notes: _initiate.py:240-242 and _discovery.py:218-221; all four fields exist on DiscoveredOAuth2FlowSnapshot (installed codemie_enterprise .../discovered_flow.py:70-75) and the reason codes dcr_cache_hit/dcr_cache_miss/dcr_profile_mismatch are real (discovery/client_registration.py:71,72,89). Asserted by test_discovered_oauth2_initiate_logs_info_with_registration_fields_and_snapshot_healed_false and test_discovered_flow_resolution_logs_info_with_registration_fields.

business_review.item: AC3 - discovered-snapshot self-heal branch logs WARNING with requested vs resolved discovered_flow_id
business_review.notes: _initiate.py:164-168 logs requested_flow_id + new_flow_id; the resolved id also appears on the INFO line as discovered_flow_id + snapshot_healed. Covered by test_discovered_oauth2_initiate_heal_branch_logs_warning_with_requested_and_new_flow_id.

business_review.item: AC4 - _discovery.py logs resolved snapshot provenance once per resolution; config_error branch logs WARNING with attempted_mechanisms and failure_reasons
business_review.notes: _discovery.py:213-223 (INFO after store) and 232-239 (config_error WARNING). Both covered, and the INFO-fires-exactly-once claim is asserted in test_discovered_flow_resolution_logs_warning_on_config_error.

business_review.item: AC5 - callback entry log and identity-provider-error branch carry the same state prefix as initiate
business_review.notes: _oauth2_callback.py:482 and :525 use _common._log_state_prefix, the same helper the initiate lines use. test_callback_entry_log_state_prefix_joins_to_initiate drives one known state through initiate and then the callback and asserts the prefixes match; test_callback_idp_error_log_includes_state_prefix covers the error branch. (Triage note: the joining test is tautological - see CR-017.)

business_review.item: AC6 - UI reports result=timeout with elapsed wait to /v1/mcp-auth/oauth2/callback-diagnostics; logged at WARNING under a message distinct from bridge failures; beacon is fire-and-forget
business_review.notes: Backend branch is correct and distinct (_diagnostics.py:59-68, "MCP OAuth2 callback never observed by client", 204). UI beacon (useAuthCallbackListener.ts:108-134, called at :166) is try/catch-wrapped, sendBeacon with fetch keepalive fallback, .catch() swallowed, fired only from onIdTimeout - verified by 4 UI tests, all passing. URL `${api.BASE_URL}/v1/mcp-auth/oauth2/callback-diagnostics` matches the served route (router.py:392-400 under prefix /v1/mcp-auth) and the repo-wide `${api.BASE_URL}/v1/...` convention. Gap: waited_ms is capped at le=3_600_000 (_diagnostics.py:47) while the UI wait is admin-configurable and unbounded (MCP_AUTH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS via appInfo.ts:145), so a >1h configured timeout produces a 422 that the beacon swallows - exactly the long-wait case AC6 exists to record. AC6 also says 'elapsed wait' but the UI sends the nominal configured timeout.

business_review.item: AC7 - no secrets logged; every logged string passes through the CWE-117 sanitizer; a test asserts the full state does not appear in captured log output
business_review.notes: No secret values are logged (no client_secret / code_verifier / tokens / session_binding_hash; state is truncated), and test_static_oauth2_initiate_info_log_never_contains_full_state satisfies the test clause. The sanitizer clause fails: _common.py:146-148 `_log_state_prefix` returns `state[:12]` with no sanitization, and _oauth2_callback.py:482/:525 feed it the raw, unauthenticated, unconstrained `state` query param (router.py:369). Verified in-repo: _log_state_prefix("a\nWARNING: x forged") -> 'a\nWARNING: x', and codemie/configs/logger.py's LogFormatter does not escape newlines. Additional new log fields in _discovery.py and _initiate.py also bypass the sanitizer.

business_review.item: AC8 - a malformed authorize URL does not raise from the logging helper; the flow being observed must be unaffected by observation; covered by a test
business_review.notes: The helper itself is safe and tested (_common.py:151-163 catches ValueError; two tests assert all-None degradation). But the state is extracted by an unguarded duplicate parse before the helper is ever called - `dict(parse_qsl(urlsplit(response.auth_url).query))` at _initiate.py:114, 232, 318, 416. Verified in-repo: this expression raises ValueError('Invalid IPv6 URL') for `https://[::1/oauth2/authorize?state=abc`, after the PKCE entry is already stored, turning a valid flow into a 500. No test exercises a malformed auth_url through an initiate path.

business_review.item: AC9 - severities follow logging-patterns.md: INFO for milestones, WARNING for expected client/validation failures, distinct messages per failure class
business_review.notes: INFO on the four initiate milestones and the discovery resolution; WARNING on self-heal, both recovery-exhaustion sites (discriminated by source=precheck|exception), config_error, client timeout, and _raise_client_error (_common.py:86). Message prefixes are distinct per class and match the guide's severity table.

business_review.item: Out of scope - do not fix EPMCDME-14215 itself, only make it diagnosable
business_review.notes: No behavioral change to the callback/timeout race; all additions are log statements plus the fire-and-forget beacon.

business_review.item: Out of scope - do not change the UI timeout value or its tracking behaviour
business_review.notes: AUTH_CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and the timer/tracking logic in useAuthCallbackListener.ts are untouched; the only insertion is one void call at :166 after `delete timeoutsRef.current[authConfigId]`.

business_review.item: Out of scope - no change to the codemie-enterprise package
business_review.notes: The combined diff spans only codemie and codemie-ui; no codemie-enterprise hunk, and the snapshot/authorize-URL fields the logs consume already exist in the pinned package.

business_review.item: Out of scope - do not list a user's stored credential ids at gate time
business_review.notes: No TMS read-by-user call added anywhere in the diff.

business_review.item: Shared helpers land in _common.py: _sanitize_log_value moved there, _log_state_prefix and _describe_authorize_request added
business_review.notes: _common.py:31 (moved, with parse_qsl import at :18), :146, :151; _diagnostics.py now imports the sanitizer from _common.

business_review.item: _describe_authorize_request parses the authorize URL via urllib.parse.parse_qsl into client_id, redirect_uri, resource, scope and the authorize-endpoint host, returning a degraded description instead of raising
business_review.notes: _common.py:151-163; all values go through _sanitize_log_value before landing in the returned dict. (Triage note: the host field uses netloc rather than hostname - see CR-008.)

business_review.item: Item E2 - _raise_client_error adds a WARNING with the sanitized reason before raising, kept as its own commit
business_review.notes: _common.py:86; isolated in commit 7ee83d4585. test_raise_client_error_logs_warning_with_sanitized_details_before_raising drives a real multi-line pydantic ValidationError and asserts no CR/LF survives.

business_review.item: _diagnostics.py - widen result Literal with "timeout", add optional waited_ms and phase, branch severity to WARNING with a message distinct from bridge failures, import sanitizer from _common
business_review.notes: _diagnostics.py:25, 38, 47-48, 59-69. test_callback_diagnostics_timeout_result_logs_distinct_warning_message asserts the bridge-failure message string is absent from the timeout line.

business_review.item: Cross-repository contract - the frontend beacon payload must match the backend Pydantic model widened in the same diff, and the URL must be the one the backend serves
business_review.notes: Keys/types line up (result/auth_config_id/opener_present/waited_ms/phase) and the URL resolves to the served path. Two mismatches: waited_ms > 3_600_000 is rejected 422 while the UI value is unbounded; and the UI hardcodes opener_present:false (useAuthCallbackListener.ts:114) from the parent window, where the field's bridge-page meaning does not apply - timeout rows will read as 'opener lost' to any query keyed on that field.

business_review.item: Spec in-scope file list (5 backend source files + 2 test files, 1 UI hook + its test)
business_review.notes: The diff also changes src/codemie/enterprise/mcp_auth/router.py (:327, :428) to thread mcp_config_id into the static and SAML builders - necessary plumbing for AC1, but absent from both the spec's In-scope list and the ticket's file table.

business_review.item: Testing - per-path caplog assertions, self-heal and recovery-exhaustion WARNING assertions, a full-state-absent test, a malformed-authorize-URL test, callback state-prefix join test, result=timeout assertions, and the three UI beacon tests
business_review.notes: Every named test exists and passes (94 backend tests in the two files, 16 UI tests, all green). Coverage is narrower than the ACs it stands for: the malformed-URL test targets only the helper, never an initiate call site (the raising line at _initiate.py:114 etc. is untested), and the full-state assertions only inspect messages captured from _initiate.logger, so nothing guards the callback-side state handling.

business_review.item: Quality gates - codemie: make ruff/build/license-check/test/gitleaks; codemie-ui: lint/typecheck/test:unit/test:integration
business_review.notes: Process requirement, not a diff artifact. Within this audit only the two touched backend test files (94 passed) and the touched UI test file (16 passed) were run; the full gate suite is adjudicated in the QA stage.

standards_review.notes: All 10 commits across both repos (9 in codemie, 1 in codemie-ui) match the git-workflow.md format `EPMCDME-14226: Capital description`; no conventional-commit prefixes present.
Branch is `EPMCDME-14226`; git-workflow.md's README evidence prefers `<TICKET-ID>_short-description`. Guide does not mark branch naming as blocking, and the branch predates this change. Non-blocking.

`from __future__ import annotations` present in both modified Python modules; new helpers fully annotated with modern unions (`str | None`, `dict[str, str | None]`). No new source files added, so no Apache-2.0 license-header obligation. Ruff/build/test gates run in the separate QA stage, not adjudicated here.

Verified directly against .ai-run/guides/development/security-patterns.md. Secret handling: traced every `_raise_client_error` call site in _initiate.py, _oauth2_callback.py and _uri.py - all `details` arguments are static string literals or config-derived URLs; none carries an auth `code`, a full `state`, a token, or `session_binding_hash`. Confirmed via runtime introspection that neither `codemie_enterprise.mcp_auth.OAuth2AuthConfig` nor `SAMLAuthConfig` declares a `client_secret` field, so a pydantic ValidationError's `input_value` echo cannot leak one through the new WARNING. `details` was already returned to the caller in the ExtendedHTTPException 400 body, so server-side logging adds no new exposure class. Untrusted input: the new unauthenticated-endpoint fields fail closed (`waited_ms` bounded ge=0/le=3_600_000 -> 422, `phase` max_length=64, `result` a Literal), and both are passed through the CWE-117 sanitizer before logging.

Matches .ai-run/guides/development/logging-patterns.md: INFO for flow milestones, WARNING for expected client/validation failures. The timeout branch uses the message 'MCP OAuth2 callback never observed by client', a signature distinct from the existing 'MCP OAuth2 callback client diagnostics' bridge-failure line, satisfying the guide's distinct-failure-class rule (AC9).

findings.title: Global stubs restored in test body, not afterEach
findings.problem: All four new tests call `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` as the last statement of the test body rather than in an `afterEach`. If any assertion in a body fails, the stubbed `navigator` leaks into every subsequent test in the file. The first new test additionally calls `vi.useRealTimers()` mid-body and never restores fake timers, so timer mode leaks too unless a `beforeEach` re-establishes them.
findings.impact: A single genuine failure in the beacon tests cascades into unrelated failures across the suite, making the real regression hard to identify and eroding trust in the file's 16 green tests.
findings.recommendation: Move `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` into an `afterEach` for the describe block, and restore fake timers in the same hook (or via `vi.useFakeTimers()` in `beforeEach`) so no test body owns global cleanup.

findings.title: waited_ms is the configured timeout, unclamped
findings.problem: `reportCallbackTimeoutDiagnostics(authConfigId, resolvedTimeoutMs)` sends the nominal configured timeout, not the measured elapsed wait, and applies no clamp. AC6 requires the 'elapsed wait'. Separately, `_diagnostics.py:47` declares `waited_ms: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=0, le=3_600_000)` while the UI value derives from the admin-settable `MCP_AUTH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (`appInfo.ts:145`) through `getPositiveInteger`, which imposes no upper bound.
findings.impact: A backgrounded tab whose timer fires late is indistinguishable from a prompt timeout - precisely the class of bug this field exists to expose. And an operator configuring a timeout above 3600s makes every timeout beacon 422; because the beacon swallows all transport outcomes, the server-side record AC6 mandates disappears without a trace in exactly the long-wait scenario most worth recording. This is a cross-repo data-contract mismatch that fails silently by design.
findings.recommendation: Record a start timestamp when the timer is armed and send `Math.min(Math.max(Math.round(Date.now() - startedAt), 0), 3_600_000)`. Document the coupling between the UI timeout config and the model's `le` bound at both ends, or raise/remove the backend ceiling and rely on the plain `int` bound.

findings.title: opener_present and phase are hardcoded stub values
findings.problem: The timeout beacon always sends `opener_present: false` and `phase: 'awaiting_callback'`. On `OAuth2CallbackDiagnostics` the `opener_present` field means 'the bridge page could still see its window.opener' - a property of the popup, not of the parent hook that fires this beacon. `phase` is typed as a 64-char free string but has exactly one possible value. Both are logged verbatim at `_diagnostics.py:66`.
findings.impact: In the other diagnostics branch `opener_present=false` is a genuine failure signal; in the timeout WARNING it is a constant that means nothing, so timeout rows are indistinguishable from genuine lost-opener rows on any dashboard or query keyed on that field. On a ticket whose sole deliverable is trustworthy triage data, a field that reads as a real signal but is a stub actively misleads incident response.
findings.recommendation: Make `opener_present` optional on the backend model and omit it from the timeout payload (or send the parent's actual observation), and either drop `phase` from the timeout beacon or constrain it to a documented enum so its values carry meaning.

findings.title: sendBeacon return value ignored, fallback unreachable
findings.problem: `navigator.sendBeacon(url, blob)` is called and its boolean return is discarded, followed by an unconditional `return`. `sendBeacon` returns `false` when the payload exceeds the user agent's queue quota or the browser refuses to queue it. The `fetch(..., { keepalive: true })` branch below is therefore reachable only when `sendBeacon` is entirely absent, and no test exercises either the `false` return or the fetch path.
findings.impact: The timeout diagnostic is silently dropped and the backend never records the missing callback - the exact observation this change exists to produce - with no signal that anything was lost.
findings.recommendation: Use `if (navigator.sendBeacon(url, blob)) return;` so a `false` return falls through to the existing `fetch` keepalive path, and add tests for both the `false` return and the fetch fallback. While in this code, confirm the backend CORS config permits a preflighted `application/json` POST to `/v1/mcp-auth/oauth2/callback-diagnostics` from the app origin (low risk - the beacon fires from a live timer, not an unload handler, and eight other call sites already POST JSON to this origin - but the failure would be silent).

findings.title: Timeout beacon carries no state prefix to join on
findings.problem: The timeout beacon posts only `auth_config_id`; the backend timeout WARNING logs `auth_config_id`, `waited_ms`, `phase`, `opener_present`, `target_origin`. The join key this whole change exists to create is the state prefix (AC5), and the timeout case - where no callback ever arrived and correlation matters most - is the one case that lacks it. For discovered flows `auth_config_id` may additionally be a synthetic id, weakening the fallback join further.
findings.impact: The primary scenario the ticket sets out to diagnose (EPMCDME-14215's callback race) produces a log row that cannot be joined back to its initiate line, so an investigator cannot tell which flow timed out.
findings.recommendation: Human decision required: determine whether the hook can obtain the state (it is present in the `auth_url` returned by initiate, but the hook currently tracks flows only by `authConfigId`). If plumbing the state prefix into the hook is feasible, add it to the beacon payload and the backend model; if not, record in the spec that `auth_config_id` is the accepted join key for the timeout path and note the synthetic-id caveat for discovered flows.

findings.title: router.py modified but absent from spec in-scope list
findings.problem: The diff changes `src/codemie/enterprise/mcp_auth/router.py` at :327 and :428 to thread `mcp_config_id` into `build_oauth2_initiate_response` / `build_saml_initiate_response`. The change is correct and required to satisfy AC1, but neither the spec's 'In scope - codemie' list nor the ticket's 'Files expected to change' table names the file.
findings.impact: A scope-conformance check reports a stray file, and the spec no longer describes the change it governs - which undermines the audit trail this gate depends on and hides the fact that a shared builder signature was altered.
findings.recommendation: Add `src/codemie/enterprise/mcp_auth/router.py` to the spec's in-scope file list with a one-line note that it threads `mcp_config_id` into the two initiate builders for AC1.

findings.title: Unsanitized state reaches callback logs (CWE-117)
findings.problem: `_log_state_prefix(state)` returns `state[:12]` with no call to `_sanitize_log_value`. `_oauth2_callback.py:482` (entry INFO) and `:525` (IdP-error WARNING) pass it the raw `state` query parameter of the unauthenticated `GET /v1/mcp-auth/oauth2/callback`, which `router.py:369` declares as `str | None = Query(default=None)` with no pattern or length bound. Verified in-repo: `_log_state_prefix("a\nWARNING: x forged")` returns `'a\nWARNING: x'`, and `codemie/configs/logger.py`'s `LogFormatter` performs no newline escaping (its `format` even converts `\\n` back to a real newline). Twelve characters is enough to terminate a line and start a forged one.
findings.impact: Anyone on the internet can forge arbitrary log records at INFO and WARNING severity by calling the callback route with `?state=%0aWARNING:%20...`. This is the exact CWE-117 hazard `_sanitize_log_value` exists to close, reintroduced on the one field this ticket adds to an anonymous endpoint, and it fails AC7's requirement that every logged string pass through the sanitizer. Forged records corrupt the very audit trail this change is meant to create.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize inside `_log_state_prefix` - truncate then `_sanitize_log_value(state[:12])`, or restrict the prefix to an allowlisted charset - and guard non-str input (`return _sanitize_log_value(state[:12]) if isinstance(state, str) else None`). Add a callback-side test that posts a `state` containing CR/LF and asserts no control character survives into the emitted log line.

findings.title: _describe_authorize_request leaks userinfo and under-guards
findings.problem: Three defects in the new helper: (1) it logs `parts.netloc`, not `parts.hostname`, and `netloc` includes any userinfo component, so an authorize URL of the form `https://user:secret@idp.example.com/authorize` writes `as_host=user:secret@idp.example.com` into an INFO line - and for the discovered flow the authorization endpoint comes from remote AS metadata, not from this system. (2) The docstring claims 'Never raises (AC8)' but the except clause catches only `ValueError`; `urlsplit(None)` or any non-str `auth_url` raises `AttributeError`/`TypeError`. (3) Space-bearing values are emitted unquoted, so a two-value OAuth2 scope logs as `scope=openid profile` and breaks key=value parsing. Values are also never truncated, while `scope`/`resource`/`redirect_uri` for a discovered flow originate from remote AS metadata.
findings.impact: Operator credentials embedded in a configured authorize URL land in central logs; the helper whose entire purpose is to never break its caller can still raise on non-str input; and mis-fielded or oversized log lines defeat the log joins this whole change exists to enable.
findings.recommendation: Use `parts.hostname` (append `:{parts.port}` if the port matters), widen the except to `except Exception` to match the documented contract, quote space-bearing values (`f'"{_sanitize_log_value(raw)}"'`), and cap each field's length the way `_diagnostics.py` already does with `max_length`.

findings.title: New discovery and initiate log fields bypass the sanitizer
findings.problem: The new log statements interpolate remote- and user-controlled strings without `_sanitize_log_value` and without any length cap: `_discovery.py:213-223` logs `mcp_config_name` (user-authored free text), `resolution.snapshot.issuer`, `as_hostname`, `canonical_resource` and the `registration_*` fields; the `config_error` WARNING at `:232-239` logs `attempted_mechanisms` and `failure_reasons` straight from `error_context`, populated from remote discovery/registration responses; `_initiate.py:166` logs `requested_flow_id` (a caller-supplied `discovered_flow_id`) and `:234-242` repeats the snapshot fields.
findings.impact: An authenticated user can forge log records via `mcp_config_name` or an unknown `discovered_flow_id` containing CR/LF, and can inflate log volume without bound with a megabyte-long value; a hostile or misconfigured authorization server can do the same through discovery metadata. AC7 requires every logged string to pass through the CWE-117 sanitizer, and the sanitizer's own docstring rationale ('the runtime environment's escaping cannot be relied on') applies identically here.
findings.recommendation: Route every newly logged string through `_sanitize_log_value` and truncate to a documented bound - e.g. `_sanitize_log_value(discovered_flow_id)[:128]` at `_initiate.py:166` and `:237`, and the same treatment for `mcp_config_name`, `issuer`, `as_hostname`, `canonical_resource`, `attempted_mechanisms` and `failure_reasons`.

findings.title: Resolution INFO log sits inside the guarded try block
findings.problem: The new `logger.info(...)` at `_discovery.py:213-223` is placed after `store(resolution.snapshot)` but still inside the `try` whose trailing broad `except` returns `_build_discovered_failure_payload(..., "discovered_flow_resolution_failed")`. Any exception raised while building that f-string - a snapshot shape lacking `registration_profile_fingerprint` or `registration_reason_code`, for instance - is swallowed and converted into a user-visible failure.
findings.impact: A purely observational statement can downgrade an already-stored, successful resolution into a failed one for the end user. This is the same 'observation breaks the observed flow' violation AC8 forbids, on the discovery path.
findings.recommendation: Move the `logger.info(...)` call below the `except` blocks so it runs only after the `try` succeeds, or wrap it in its own `try/except Exception: pass`. Note the fields themselves are confirmed present on the installed `DiscoveredOAuth2FlowSnapshot`, so the concern is the structural exposure, not a known-missing attribute.

findings.title: config_error branch assumes error_context is a Mapping
findings.problem: The new `config_error` WARNING calls `error_context.get("attempted_mechanisms")` and `.get("failure_reasons")`. Adjacent pre-existing code writes `resolution.error_context or {}` before passing it to the payload builder, which indicates the value can be falsy or `None`; a `None` or non-Mapping `error_context` makes `.get` raise `AttributeError` inside the error branch.
findings.impact: An `AttributeError` in the `config_error` branch turns a structured 4xx-shaped failure payload into a 500, degrading exactly the error path this logging was added to illuminate.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the shape of `resolution.error_context` at this call site; if it can be `None` or non-Mapping, coerce once with `error_context = resolution.error_context or {}` before the log statement and reuse that local for both the log and the payload builder.

findings.title: Unguarded authorize-URL parse can 500 a successful initiate
findings.problem: Four initiate paths run `dict(parse_qsl(urlsplit(response.auth_url).query)).get(...)` with no try/except - `_initiate.py:114` (static), `:232` (discovered), `:318` (recovery), `:416` (SAML) - immediately before calling the deliberately non-raising `_describe_authorize_request`. Verified in-repo: `urlsplit("https://[::1/oauth2/authorize?state=abc")` raises `ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL`. The defensive wrapper was placed on the helper but not on the identical parse one line above it, and the same three-line block is copy-pasted into all four functions.
findings.impact: These lines run after `_build_enterprise_initiate_response` has already minted the state and written the PKCE entry, so a malformed authorize endpoint converts a flow that actually succeeded into a 500 - the user loses a working authorization purely because of a logging statement. This is precisely what AC8 forbids, and no test drives a malformed `auth_url` through an initiate path.
findings.recommendation: Have `_describe_authorize_request` also return the `state`/`RelayState` value so there is one guarded parse instead of two, removing both the duplication across four functions and the unguarded call. Add a test that drives a malformed `auth_url` (e.g. `https://[::1/oauth2/authorize?state=abc`) through an initiate path and asserts the response still returns successfully.

findings.title: snapshot_healed reports attempt, not success
findings.problem: `snapshot_healed = True` is assigned unconditionally when `_probe is None`, before `ensure_discovered_snapshot_for_server` runs, and is never reset when `_new_flow_id is None` (heal failed) or when the re-probe still returns `None`. The WARNING message says 'heal attempted' while the INFO field is named `snapshot_healed` - two names for the same fact, one of them false.
findings.impact: Anyone reading `snapshot_healed=true` in production concludes a self-heal succeeded when it may have failed, sending incident triage down the wrong path on the exact signal this ticket added to guide it.
findings.recommendation: Set the flag from the outcome (`snapshot_healed = _new_flow_id is not None`), or rename the field to `heal_attempted` and add a separate `heal_succeeded` boolean so the log line and the WARNING agree.

findings.title: Discovered and recovery lines omit the auth_config_id join key
findings.problem: `_initiate.py:236` emits the auth-config id as `discovered_auth_id={snapshot.discovered_auth_id}`, while `_discovery.py:215` and `_oauth2_callback.py:522` emit the identical value as `auth_config_id=` (confirmed: `codemie_enterprise/mcp_auth/discovered_flow.py:350` sets `auth_config_id=discovered_auth_id`). The recovery line at `_initiate.py:320-325` omits the auth-config id altogether. AC1 names `auth_config_id` for every initiate path.
findings.impact: A log query keyed on `auth_config_id=<id>` silently misses every discovered initiate and every recovery initiate, so two of the four flows cannot be joined to their own discovery and callback lines. That defeats the central deliverable of the ticket while the INFO lines look present and correct.
findings.recommendation: Emit `auth_config_id=` on the discovered line (keep `discovered_auth_id=` as an additional alias only if something already depends on it), and add the recovery flow's auth-config id if the enterprise response exposes it; if it genuinely cannot be sourced there, record that limitation in the spec.

findings.title: SAML initiate logged under the OAuth2 message prefix
findings.problem: The SAML path logs `"MCP OAuth2 initiate issued: flow=saml"` and labels the SAML `RelayState` as `state=`. Because `_describe_authorize_request` is OAuth2-shaped, the line also emits `client_id=None redirect_uri=None resource=None scope=None` on every SAML initiate, and `test_saml_initiate_logs_info_with_state_prefix_and_authorize_fields` asserts each of those None fields, cementing the noise.
findings.impact: A log search for 'MCP OAuth2 initiate' now returns SAML flows and an OAuth2 investigation surfaces SAML noise - on a ticket whose deliverable is a queryable log taxonomy, conflating two protocols under one message prefix degrades every future query. Four dead fields per SAML line add volume without information.
findings.recommendation: Use a distinct message prefix for the SAML path (e.g. 'MCP SAML initiate issued'), label the field `relay_state=` rather than `state=`, and omit the four always-None OAuth2 fields from the SAML line - updating the test to assert their absence instead of their None value.

findings.title: Required kwarg added to shared builders without a call-site sweep
findings.problem: `build_oauth2_initiate_response` and `build_saml_initiate_response` gained a *required* keyword argument `mcp_config_id`, and only two call sites were updated (`router.py:327` and `:428`). These are bridge functions re-exported through `dependencies`, and the `_enabled` suffix on the updated call sites implies disabled/fallback counterparts. Any other caller - another router, a workflow or agent recovery path, an untouched test - now fails with `TypeError` at runtime, and the diff provides no evidence the sweep was exhaustive. `test_build_saml_initiate_passes_mcp_config_id_as_required_param` merely asserts `pytest.raises(TypeError)`, which tests CPython argument binding rather than this system's behavior.
findings.impact: A pure-observability change introduces a hard runtime break on any unswept caller, in code paths that may only execute during an auth failure or recovery - the worst time to discover a `TypeError`.
findings.recommendation: Grep both repos for every call to the two builders and confirm each passes `mcp_config_id`; the zero-risk alternative is to give the parameter a `None` default and drop the `pytest.raises(TypeError)` test. In the same pass, grep for imports of `_sanitize_log_value` from `_diagnostics` - the symbol moved to `_common`, so any remaining importer of its old home breaks at import time.

findings.title: AC5/AC7/AC8 tests pass for the wrong reasons
findings.problem: Three of the tests standing in as AC evidence do not exercise what they claim. `test_callback_entry_log_state_prefix_joins_to_initiate` patches `shared_logger.info` *after* the initiate call, so the initiate line is never captured; it then asserts the callback line contains `_log_state_prefix(known_state)` - comparing the helper against itself on a state it chose. `test_describe_authorize_request_returns_all_none_on_malformed_url` uses `urlsplit("not a url::")`, which does not raise - it returns an empty netloc and query, so every field becomes None through the happy path, and the test would keep passing if the try/except were deleted. The state fixtures are single repeated characters (`"j"*40`, `"e"*40`, ...), so `state[:12]` is always a run of one character.
findings.impact: Green tests are being read as AC5/AC7/AC8 evidence they do not provide, which is how the defects in CR-007 and CR-012 reached this gate. The degenerate fixtures also mean no test can detect the practical failure mode where a structured or signed state has a constant 12-character header, making the join key identical across all users and flows.
findings.recommendation: Capture the initiate log line before the callback so the join test actually compares two independently emitted lines; use an input that genuinely raises (e.g. `http://[::1`) in the malformed-URL test; and replace the repeated-character fixtures with realistic base64 signed-state values so the tests verify that 12 characters actually discriminate between flows.
